entries.f: The trail stands in town, off Main Street, with trailhead posts on Webster Street and Pheasant Lane. Its two linked walks — 0.6 miles on the north side, 1 mile on the south — run in the wash under broken cliffs, past an old concrete water pipe left over from the town's early days. The wash is greener in the wet months, with big rocks to scramble, wildlife tracks in the sand, and thorny plants to step around. Easy on the north side, moderate on the south.
entries.d: less than 10 minutes from the Hearth — 5 minutes by road, a mile and a half

more.hiking: For the hiker: the walk runs in the wash under broken cliffs, past an old concrete water pipe from the town's early days — easy on the north side, moderate on the south, with big rocks to scramble.
more.walking: For the walker: two linked walks near Main Street — 0.6 miles on the north side, 1 mile on the south — greener in the wet months, with wildlife tracks in the sand.

more.biking: For the rider: the south section is open to every kind of traveler, and the county's riding page rates it difficult for bikes — Payson's steep ground shows here.

entries.f: In town, the loop runs 2.4 miles through the pale granite of the Granite Dells, past whitish, tooth-like boulders, with trees pressed close and mountains beyond. Wildflowers bloom in spring, and javelina are about. Moderate.

more.trail: For the trail-seeker: the path runs 3.7 miles from the Event Center to the Peach Orchard Trailhead.

entries.f: North of town on Houston Mesa Road, the trail runs about 1.6 miles out and back, up the East Verde River to the falls, the swimming holes, and the old rusted water wheel that gave the place its name. A federal day-use pass is required — a Tonto pass: $8 per vehicle for the day at a Forest Service office or a store that sells them, $12 at the fee machine, and the machines take debit or credit cards. The fee machines for this ground stand at Shoefly Village, Houston Mesa Campground, and the Payson Ranger Station. The Forest Service gives no months for the fee (TBD).
entries.d: about a 25-minute ride from the Hearth — 10 miles by road

entries.f: The trail runs out and back for 9.2 miles along Horton Creek, through old-growth ponderosa and ferns, climbing the Rim's face to Horton Springs at mile five. Hard. NOTE WELL: the trailhead parking stands closed for bridge work on Tonto Creek through December 31, 2026 — begin instead at the Derrick Trailhead.
entries.d: about a 40-minute ride from the Hearth — 20 miles by road

more.bird watching: For the bird watcher: the creek trail has its own eBird hotspot. The records birders have left from this creek name the Mexican Jay, the Pacific Wren, and the Red-breasted Nuthatch among the pines and falls.
more.hiking: For the hiker: 9.2 miles out and back along the creek, climbing the Rim's face to Horton Springs at mile five — hard. The trailhead parking stands closed through 2026; begin at the Derrick Trailhead.
more.water: For the water-lover: Horton Creek runs beside the trail its whole length, up to the springs at mile five.
more.creek: For the creek-walker: the trail follows Horton Creek through old-growth ponderosa and ferns, all the way up the Rim's face.
more.fishing: For the angler: the creek is a trout water — its pools are fished along the trail under the ponderosas. A license may be required — check before you go that you hold a valid Arizona fishing license.
more.trail: For the trail-seeker: the path follows Horton Creek 9.2 miles out and back, up the face of the Rim.

entries.f: The trail runs 7.6 miles up a creek canyon by Christopher Creek, to the top of the Rim. Ferns, vine maples, old fruit trees, and mushrooms after the rains line the way. The canyon is loved above all in fall, when the leaves turn red and gold.
entries.d: about a 40-minute ride from the Hearth — 23 miles by road

more.bird watching: For the bird watcher: the town's own birding page names this trailhead for its creek ground and mixed forest. Birders camped by the trailhead recorded warblers of four kinds, painted redstarts, hermit thrushes, and broad-tailed hummingbirds.
more.hiking: For the hiker: 7.6 miles up a creek canyon by Christopher Creek to the top of the Rim — ferns, vine maples, and old fruit trees.
more.water: For the water-lover: the creek runs the canyon beside you the whole climb.
more.creek: For the creek-walker: the trail climbs beside the creek from Christopher Creek to the Rim's top.
more.trail: For the trail-seeker: the path climbs 7.6 miles up the canyon by Christopher Creek to the top of the Rim.
more.fall colors: For the fall-color seeker: in fall the vine maples turn red and gold up the canyon — the color walk this country is known for.

entries.f: The town's great green at the end of Main Street — 43 acres built around three lakes, stocked for fishing (a license is needed) and open to your own kayak or canoe. Around the water stand a splash pad for the children, a playground, shaded ramadas with grills for a day's feast, and an amphitheater that hosts summer concerts under the Rim. And the park holds more than play: the Rim Country Museum and the Zane Grey Cabin stand within it, so a traveler may walk from a morning's fishing straight into the country's own history. The name above leads to the town's own fuller word on the park.
entries.d: less than 10 minutes from the Hearth — 7 minutes by road, 2 miles

more.bird watching: For the bird watcher: this park is a named birding ground — an eBird hotspot with more than 200 kinds of birds recorded, and a stop on the Arizona Birding Trail. Ducks and Canada geese live on the three lakes, herons stalk the shallows, and bald eagles and osprey fish the stocked water, while hummingbirds, acorn woodpeckers, and vermilion flycatchers work the trees along the shore. Come early in the morning, or toward evening, when the birds are busiest.
more.water: For the water-lover: three lakes totaling some thirteen acres of water sit at the park's heart.
more.fishing: For the angler: the lakes are stocked for fishing — a license is needed, so check before you go that you hold a valid Arizona fishing license.
more.kids: Location: The splash pad and the playground stand by the lakes, ready for the children.
more.history: Location: The Zane Grey Cabin stands in the park, and the Rim Country Museum tells the country's own story.
more.picnics: For the picnicker: shaded ramadas with grills stand ready for a day's feast.
more.views: For the view-seeker: the town's tourism page names the sunsets here — three lakes under the Rim, at the day's end. The picture seat of the town's parks.
more.concerts: For the music-lover: the amphitheater hosts summer concerts under the Rim.
more.kayaking: For the paddler: your own kayak or canoe may ride the lakes.
more.museum: Location: The Rim Country Museum stands inside the park.
more.splash pad: For the splash-seeker: the town's own plan runs the splash pad from May 1 to September 30, and calls that season proposed and subject to change (TBD). Its daily hours are not settled.

entries.w: Open daily, 6 in the morning to 10:30 at night.

entries.f: The largest ground in the town's keeping — 82 acres, and full: a new disc golf course through the trees, six pickleball courts, three tennis courts, a few ball fields, sand volleyball, and basketball. A skate park for the bold, a dog park for the hounds, two playgrounds for the small folk, and bocce and horseshoes for the patient. Six ramadas with grills stand ready for gatherings, a one-mile trail rings the whole park, and the Payson Public Library itself stands inside the park — sport and story under the same pines. The name above leads to the town's own fuller word on the park.
entries.d: less than 10 minutes from the Hearth — 8 minutes by road, 2 miles

more.books: Location: The Payson Public Library stands inside this park's own grounds. It lends books for three weeks on a free county card, and holds a children's room, a teen gaming room, and a meeting room to book. The library keeps its own entry on this page, under The Town's Halls, with its hours.
more.basketball: For the basketball player: two courts stand in the park, by the town's own count.
more.dogs: Location: The enclosed dog park stands on the park's northeast side, on the Laredo street side. There, dogs may run free.
more.playgrounds: Location: Two playgrounds stand in the park. One stands on the northeast side, at 404 North Laredo Lane.
more.picnics: For the feast-keeper: six ramadas with tables and grills stand across the park, ready for a day's gathering.
more.biking: For the rider: the town's own page names the park's one-mile ring trail a hiking and mountain bike trail — riders take it around every ground in the park.
more.walking: For the walker: a one-mile trail rings the whole park, past every ground in it.
more.kids: For the children: two playgrounds stand in the park, one of them on the northeast side.
more.indoors: Location: The Payson Public Library stands inside the park, with reading rooms and story times under the same pines.
more.trail: For the trail-seeker: a one-mile trail rings the whole park, past every ground in it — the town's own page names it a hiking and mountain bike trail.
more.ball fields: For the ball player: a few ball fields stand among the park's sports grounds, and a football field stands at the park's center — baseball and softball under the Rim.
more.bocce: Location: The bocce court stands west of the tennis courts, close to the restrooms. It is the park's one full-size court, 60 feet by 10. The town built it in 2021 at the asking of a local seniors' group, and the court can be reserved through the town.
more.disc golf: Location: The disc golf course runs across the park's middle. It is a new course of 18 holes, over hilly ground through the trees.
more.horseshoes: For the horseshoe pitcher: two pits stand in the park, apart from the bocce court.
more.pickleball: Location: The six pickleball courts stand on the park's north side, beside the tennis courts — four beside them, and two more uphill above them. Bring your paddle and take your turn.
more.skate park: Location: The skate park stands on the park's northwest side. Its steel ramps stand on a concrete slab: a half pipe, quarter pipes, banked ramps, a spine ramp, two grind rails, and a fun box with a rail. Lights stand over the ramps, so the skating runs on past sunset, until the park closes.
more.tennis: Location: The three tennis courts stand on the park's north side, a little west of its center. The pickleball courts stand beside them, and the bocce court just west of them.
more.volleyball: For the volleyball player: two sand courts stand among the park's sports grounds.

entries.f: Bigger-than-life wildlife in bright colors stands painted by local artists on the corrugated fence along the American Gulch walking path: javelina, roadrunner, squirrel, coyote, rabbit, and two elk locking antlers.

more.art: For the art-seeker: bigger-than-life wildlife in bright colors runs along the corrugated fence.
more.murals: For the mural-seeker: javelina, roadrunner, squirrel, coyote, rabbit, and two elk locking antlers — painted on the fence.
more.walking: For the walker: the mural lines the American Gulch walking path itself — the art keeps you company on the walk.
more.wildlife: For the wildlife-seeker: the painted wildlife is the wildlife of this country — javelina, coyote, roadrunner, rabbit, and elk.

entries.f: Painted elk statues stand around town. The cost of each is borne by a local business, program, or neighbor, and painted by an artist with its own story of this country. One stands at Banner Payson Medical Center, and more are bound for Main Street. The herd is still growing; its own write-up stands below.
